"Barrier" is, regretfully, a remarkably overloaded term, with different meanings in (at least) the sub-disciplines of architectural memory models (ordering of load and store operations from multiple initiators), concurrent programming (synchronization of thread group execution), and garbage collection (mutator behaviors required for preserving system invariants).

The Cornucopia Reloaded paper...
- uses the word "barrier" to mean this latter sense;
- goes so far as to explicitly compare the CD-tracking feature of PTEs with traditional GC store barriers (though it points out that its machinery is somewhat unusual, being an architectural primitive and not code inserted by a compiler on behalf of a runtime system); and
- continues to rely on CD-tracking to know which pages must have their CRGs maintained, though this is a performance optimization and not required for correctness as it was in Cornucopia.

That said... surely this whole "Capability Revocation" section should be marked as informative (and not normative)?
- "{cheri_priv_crg_ext} adds capability revocation for userspace pages only"; no, it adds _a primitive that is useful for software implementation of_ capability revocation.  (CHERI+MTE and CHERIoT _might_ be able to make the claim of adding revocation in an architectural sense, but, IMHO, only sort of... in any case, surely Svucrg should not make that claim.)
- "which needs sweeping (...)" is definitely a software perspective on the matter; barring subsequent extension or platform machinery (such as CHERIoT's revocation engine or a CHERI+MTE analogue), architecture does not know what "sweeping" means or why it might be needed.
